title: File the annual unclaimed property holder report (Illinois)
description: Businesses holding property that has gone unclaimed — uncashed payroll or vendor checks, customer credits and refunds, unused gift cards, deposits — must report and turn it over to the state each year, after sending the owner a due diligence notice before the deadline. The annual report and payment are due May 1 for general property. Report before May 1; payment is made when the report is uploaded. A negative report is required only of business holders with sales over $1 million, publicly traded securities, net worth over $10 million or more than 100 employees. One vendor source gives April 30 for corporations and October 31 for financial institutions. Which state's law applies depends on the owner's last known address, or the business's state of incorporation when there is none, so a business can owe reports to several states.

feeDetail.note: There is no fee to file or register.

title: Put freelance work of $500 or more in a written contract (Illinois)
description: Under the Freelance Worker Protection Act (from July 1, 2024), hiring a freelancer for $500 or more, counting contracts in a 120-day window, requires a written contract with both parties' contact information, the scope of work, payment terms and deadlines (the department publishes a model contract). Keep it two years and pay within 30 days of completion. A missing contract costs the greater of $500 or the contract value in statutory damages; late payment costs double the underpayment plus fees; the Attorney General can seek up to $5,000 per violation.

feeDetail.note: There is no fee; this is a contracting requirement.

penalty.note: Statutory damages of the greater of $500 or the contract value for a missing contract; the Attorney General can seek up to $5,000 per violation.

title: Classify contractors correctly for unemployment insurance (Illinois)
description: Under section 212 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, services for pay are employment unless the business proves the worker is free from its control and direction and the work is outside its usual course or places of business; the exemption is much narrower than the common idea of an independent contractor. Misclassification costs back contributions, 24% interest, penalties and possible personal liability for officers. Construction workers fall under the separate Employee Classification Act.

feeDetail.note: There is no fee; this is a contracting requirement.
